metaDescription: Six long-handle fruit grabbers compared, from a compact 66 inch steel kit to a 26 foot aluminum pole, for picking fruit without climbing a ladder.
introParagraphs: A fruit grabber is the simplest answer to a common backyard problem: the best fruit is always just out of reach. A pole with a cushioned basket or claw on the end lets you collect it from the ground, which is safer than a stepladder and gentler on knees, shoulders and balance. The catch is that grabbers vary enormously, from a short kit for a patio citrus tree to a telescoping pole that runs past 20 feet.

The six picks here cover that spread. The Lilyvane 66 inch kit and the DonSail 35 to 65 inch pole are the compact options. The BlumeTrec 6.5FT and the Suchtale 8FT sit in the middle. The Suchtale 13FT steps up to long steel reach, and the TONYINGO 26FT is an aluminum telescoping pole that locks at set heights. Most use a foam-lined basket, and the DonSail adds a claw-style head for catching and pulling.

We evaluated each pick from its listing specs and typical buyer feedback, so measurements and materials are as the makers describe them. Whichever grabber you choose, treat every metal pole as a conductor and keep it clear of overhead wires. A grabber that is too long for your yard is a hazard, not a bonus.

products.name: Lilyvane 66 Inch Fruit Picker with Fruit Basket
products.description:
The Lilyvane is the most complete small kit in this lineup. The listing says the package contains a long pole in several sections, a basket, a foam pad and a carry bag, which means there is nothing extra to buy. The basket attaches to the pole with adjustable clamps rather than a thread, so it can fit several pole diameters, and the steel sections splice together to a total length of 66 inches.

That length, just under 5 and a half feet, makes it a tool for low branches rather than tall trees. Stand on the ground and your reach adds up to roughly 10 or 11 feet, which covers a dwarf peach, a trellised pear or the lower limbs of a lemon tree. Because the clamp holds the basket in place without threading, assembly is quick. The carry bag is also a practical detail, since a pole with loose sections tends to get lost.

The tradeoff is a ceiling. At 66 inches, the Lilyvane cannot match the Suchtale 13FT or the TONYINGO, and the splicing joints are a point to watch if you lift a heavy fruit. It is a better fit than the DonSail 35 to 65 inch pole if you want a bag and pad included. Check the clamp before each lift, and store the sections together in the bag so they stay a set.
products.bestFor: Small trees and low branches where a complete kit with a carry bag is more useful than extra reach.
pros: Basket, pad and bag all included
Clamp fits several pole diameters
Steel sections feel sturdy
Quick to assemble and pack away
cons: 66 inches will not reach a tall crown
Spliced joints need checking under load

products.name: DonSail Fruit Picker Pole Tool, 35 to 65 Inch
products.description:
The DonSail 35 to 65 inch grabber has the shortest reach in this guide, and it is aimed at a particular user. It adjusts piece by piece to 35, 40 or 65 inches, which the maker describes as 3 to 5 feet, so it is a hand-and-arm extension rather than a high-reach pole. The head is a twist-on metal basket with a claw, roughly 9 by 5.5 by 5.5 inches, designed for avocados, tangerines and similar fruit.

A short, thick shaft is a virtue when precision matters. The 1 inch stainless steel tube is firm, so the claw stays where you aim it, and the whole tool is light enough to use one-handed for short stretches. It suits a patio citrus tree, a potted avocado or a shrub with fruit just above your head. Because it is so short, there is little risk of the pole swaying into a wire.

The obvious limit is height. Next to the Lilyvane at 66 inches, the DonSail's 65 inch top setting is nearly identical, though the DonSail has a larger, claw-style head and the Lilyvane includes a bag and pad. If you need more than 10 feet of total reach, step up to the Suchtale or TONYINGO. Keep the basket dry after each use, since the wire can rust if left damp.
products.bestFor: Patio fruit trees and low branches where a short, precise reach is enough.
pros: Thick 1 inch steel shaft stays steady
Claw head helps pull fruit toward you
Three length settings are easy to set
Short enough to use in tight spaces
cons: Basket lacks a listed foam pad

products.name: BlumeTrec 6.5FT Fruit Picker with Basket
products.description:
The BlumeTrec 6.5FT is a short stainless steel grabber that extends from 35 to 77 inches. A thick foam pad lines the bottom of the basket, giving each fruit a soft landing, and the maker markets it for apples and mangoes alike. The sections are built so the length can be adjusted to suit the branch, and the whole kit is small enough to hang on a garage hook.

What sets it apart from the DonSail 35 to 65 inch grabber is the padding. A claw can catch a fruit, but a foam-lined basket absorbs the impact of a drop, which matters for peaches, pears and figs. It also gives you about a foot more length, which helps when the fruit is just above the top of your reach. The shaft is light enough that most users can pick for long stretches without tiring.

The limit is the same as any short pole: 77 inches will not get to the second tier of a full-size tree. If that is your situation, the Suchtale 8FT adds about 18 inches of length, and the Suchtale 13FT adds far more. Wipe the sections down after use, keep the foam dry and avoid forcing a stubborn fruit loose, because a twist of the wrist is safer than a hard tug.
products.bestFor: Dwarf trees and trellised fruit where a foam-padded landing matters most.
pros: Thick foam pad cushions each fruit
Stainless steel sections resist rust
77 inch top length is easy to aim
Compact enough to hang in a garage
cons: Cannot reach a standard tree crown

products.name: Suchtale 8FT Fruit Picker Tool
products.description:
The Suchtale 8FT reaches 95 inches, which is just under 8 feet. Each section is 1.4 feet long, so you can build the length up in small steps rather than jumping from a short pole to a long one. The listing calls it a fruit grabber, describes a protective foam pad, and says the stainless steel is rust-resistant. Apples, cherries, peaches, avocados and mangoes are the fruit the maker lists.

This is the tool for a medium tree. With a standing reach of roughly 6 feet added to 95 inches of pole, you can get to the upper branches of a semi-dwarf apple or pear. The small sections give you fine control over length, so you set the pole to the branch and avoid carrying extra weight. The foam pad makes it gentler than a bare wire basket for soft fruit.

Compared with the BlumeTrec 6.5FT, you gain about a foot and a half of reach at little extra weight. Compared with the Suchtale 13FT, you give up about 5 feet but gain much better handling. Remember to wipe the sap from each section before storage, and avoid using any steel pole in wet weather or near overhead lines.
products.bestFor: Semi-dwarf apple, pear and citrus trees that need about 8 feet of pole.
pros: 1.4 foot sections allow fine length steps
Rust-resistant stainless steel
Protective foam pad softens landings
Handles apples, peaches and mangoes
cons: Stops short of a full-size tree crown
Metal pole must stay clear of wires

products.name: Suchtale 13FT Fruit Picker Tool
products.description:
The Suchtale 13FT is the same family as the 8FT, stretched to 158 inches, or roughly 13 feet. It keeps the same 1.4 foot sections, the same protective foam pad and the same rust-resistant stainless steel, so the tool feels familiar. The difference is simply how many sections you add.

The benefit of the shared design is that you can start short and add pieces as the harvest moves higher into the tree. On the lower branches you use a few sections and enjoy easy handling. Near the top you add sections one by one and brace the butt against your hip. That progressive approach is more comfortable than a telescoping pole that gives you only a few fixed lengths, and the foam still cushions fruit all the way up.

The weight at the tip is the cost. With 158 inches of steel in your hands and a fruit in the basket, the pole demands both arms and a steady stance. For lighter handling at a similar height, the TONYINGO aluminum pole is an easier carry, but its telescoping locks need more checking. If your tree is under 12 feet tall, the Suchtale 8FT will be easier to live with. Always look up for wires before extending.
products.bestFor: Tall fruit trees where you want to grow the pole one small section at a time.
pros: Reach to 158 inches in small steps
Foam pad protects delicate fruit
Stainless steel resists rust
Same sections as the shorter Suchtale
cons: Heavy to steer at full length

products.name: TONYINGO 26FT Reach Fruit Picker Pole with Basket
products.description:
The TONYINGO 26FT is the grabber for very tall trees. It telescopes from 5 to 20 feet and locks at five stops: 5, 9, 12, 16 and 20 feet. The maker states a reach of 26 feet when your own height is added. The listing describes a large metal basket measuring 5.7 by 13 inches, which is a longer, deeper shape than the other baskets here and helps catch fruit that would otherwise bounce out.

Telescoping poles are quick to set. You twist or flip a lock and slide to the next stop, with no pieces to assemble and no bag of sections to carry. That makes the TONYINGO the easiest of the long grabbers to use across several trees of different heights. The fixed stops also make the length repeatable from one session to the next, so you learn which setting suits which tree.

The drawbacks are weight at length and electrical conductivity. A 20 foot pole is heavy to hold even when it is aluminum, and a wire that is 20 feet away is within reach of the tip. Compared with the Suchtale 13FT, the TONYINGO offers much higher reach but needs more care, and the locks must be checked before every lift. Do not use it near power lines or in wet weather.
products.bestFor: Large old trees and mixed gardens where one pole must cover many heights.
pros: Reaches 20 feet of pole length
Five fixed stops make length repeatable
Large deep basket catches rolling fruit
No sections to assemble or lose
cons: Long pole is tiring to hold
Aluminum is a conductor near wires

buyingCriteria.explanation: Reach is pole length plus your own standing reach, which for most adults is about 6 feet. The Lilyvane at 66 inches and the DonSail at 65 inches give you roughly 11 feet of total height. The Suchtale 8FT at 95 inches gives about 14 feet, the Suchtale 13FT at 158 inches about 19 feet, and the TONYINGO at 20 feet of pole about 26 feet. Measure the fruit you want before buying, and add one section as a margin.

A grabber is only as gentle as its head. The BlumeTrec 6.5FT and both Suchtale models list a foam pad, the Lilyvane includes a separate pad, and the TONYINGO has a large metal basket measuring 5.7 by 13 inches. The DonSail uses a claw-style metal basket. For soft fruit such as peaches and figs, favor a padded model. For firm citrus or avocados, a claw or bare basket is acceptable.

Sectional poles, such as the Suchtale 8FT and 13FT, are built from 1.4 foot pieces that you stack. They are secure and let you fine-tune length. Telescoping poles, such as the TONYINGO, extend in one motion and lock at 5, 9, 12, 16 and 20 feet. They are faster but depend on locks that need checking. If you pick in one spot, sectional is fine. If you move between trees, telescoping saves time.

Leverage is the hidden cost of reach. A fruit in a basket at 158 inches feels far heavier than the same fruit at 65 inches. A short pole like the DonSail or BlumeTrec 6.5FT can be held one-handed for a minute. A long steel pole like the Suchtale 13FT needs both hands, and the TONYINGO at 20 feet is easier to carry but harder to steady. Choose the shortest pole that reaches.

How the head joins the pole matters for security. The Lilyvane uses adjustable clamps that fit several pole diameters. The DonSail, BlumeTrec and TONYINGO use a twist-on thread. A thread is secure but fixed, and a clamp is flexible but needs checking. If you plan to swap heads later or use a pole you already own, the clamp or standard thread gives you more choice.

All six grabbers are made of metal. Look up before you extend any section, and keep the pole at least three metres, about ten feet, away from any overhead line. Never use the pole in damp conditions or near a branch that touches a wire. If your tree is close to a service drop, choose a short pole, or ask a professional to pick the high fruit.

howWeEvaluated.title: Reach and range
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared each pole's listed length with the heights of common home fruit trees. The Lilyvane and DonSail lead for low fruit at 66 and 65 inches, the Suchtale 8FT and BlumeTrec cover medium trees, and the Suchtale 13FT and TONYINGO lead for tall trees at 158 inches and 20 feet.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fruit protection
howWeEvaluated.description: Foam padding and basket shape both affect bruising. The BlumeTrec 6.5FT, Suchtale models and Lilyvane list padding, the TONYINGO adds a deep basket, and the DonSail relies on a claw and a metal basket. Picks that list padding scored higher for soft fruit.

howWeEvaluated.title: Control and weight
howWeEvaluated.description: A grabber that wobbles loses fruit and tires the arms. We looked at shaft thickness, such as the DonSail's 1 inch steel, and at how length changes handling across the lineup. The shorter poles scored best for control, while the long poles scored on reach.

howWeEvaluated.title: Adjustment and setup
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared the 1.4 foot sections of the Suchtale models, the splice design of the Lilyvane, the fixed lock stops of the TONYINGO and the three settings of the DonSail. Poles that are quick to set and easy to check scored higher for everyday use.

howWeEvaluated.title: Completeness of the kit
howWeEvaluated.description: The Lilyvane includes a basket, pad and bag, while the DonSail and BlumeTrec ship as pole and head. We credited kits that need nothing extra, and noted that none of the six is a head-only listing.

faq.q: What is the difference between a fruit grabber and a fruit picker?
faq.a: The terms overlap, and most listings use them interchangeably. A grabber usually means a pole with a basket or claw that catches fruit, while a picker may also include a cutting head. The six here are all pole-and-basket designs. Check the head type in the listing, because a claw behaves differently from a padded basket.

faq.q: How long a grabber do I need for a typical backyard tree?
faq.a: Add about 6 feet of standing reach to the pole length. For a dwarf tree, the DonSail at 65 inches or the Lilyvane at 66 inches reaches about 11 feet. For a semi-dwarf tree, the Suchtale 8FT reaches about 14 feet. For a standard tree, the Suchtale 13FT or the TONYINGO is the right size.

faq.q: Are these grabbers safe to use near power lines?
faq.a: No. Every pole here is steel or aluminum, and both conduct electricity. Keep at least three metres, about ten feet, from any overhead line, and never use the pole in damp weather near one. If your tree touches a wire, call the utility rather than moving the branch yourself.

faq.q: Will a grabber damage the fruit?
faq.a: A foam-padded basket, as on the BlumeTrec and Suchtale models, reduces bruising, but rough handling still causes damage. Lift gently, do not fill the basket to the top, and lower the pole before you empty it. A claw head, like the DonSail's, is best for firm fruit.

faq.q: Can I use a grabber for fruit other than apples?
faq.a: Yes. The DonSail lists avocados and tangerines, the Suchtale models list cherries, peaches and mangoes, and the BlumeTrec lists apples and mangoes. The main limits are the basket size and the weight of the fruit. Very large fruit such as pomelos need a deeper basket and a firmer pole.

faq.q: How do I store a sectional pole?
faq.a: Take the sections apart, wipe off sap and moisture, and store them together in a dry place. The Lilyvane comes with a bag for this purpose. For telescoping poles like the TONYINGO, retract fully and hang the pole by one end. Avoid damp sheds, where steel can rust.

faq.q: Is a longer pole always better?
faq.a: No. Leverage increases quickly with length, so a long pole is harder to aim and more tiring to hold. The best grabber is the shortest one that reaches your fruit. If you only have a dwarf tree, the BlumeTrec 6.5FT is easier to live with than the TONYINGO.
